'''Javon Alexander Mack'''<ref>{{cite web | title=ESPN Profile | work= ESPN.com | url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/player/_/id/12616 }}</ref> (born November 19, 1985)<ref>{{cite web| url = https://www.californiabirthindex.org/birth/javon_alexander_mack_born_1985_17480247| title = Reference at www.californiabirthindex.org}}{{Dead link|date=June 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Center (gridiron football)|center]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[California Golden Bears football|California Golden Bears]] and was selected by the [[Cleveland Browns]] in the first round with the 21st overall selection of the [[2009 NFL draft]]. He also played for the [[Atlanta Falcons]] and the [[San Francisco 49ers]]. He was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2025.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://footballfoundation.org/news/2025/1/15/nff-announces-all-star-2025-college-football-hall-of-fame-class.aspx | title=NFF Announces All-Star 2025 College Football Hall of Fame Class | publisher=[[National Football Foundation]] | date=January 15, 2025 | accessdate=16 January 2025}}</ref>

==Early life==
Mack was born in Los Angeles, California. He attended [[San Marcos High School (Santa Barbara, California)|San Marcos High School]] in [[Santa Barbara, California|Santa Barbara]], where he was named the Channel League's Co-Most Valuable Player on defense and earned a first-team all-league selection.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Plaschke |first=Bill |author-link=Bill Plaschke |date=February 3, 2017 |title=Not forgotten: For every Super Bowl star, there's an equally talented player who didn't make it |url=https://www.latimes.com/sports/la-sp-mack-falcons-plaschke-20170203-story.html |access-date=January 7, 2018 |work=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US |issn=0458-3035}}</ref> He was also selected to the All-CIF team. In addition to football, Mack wrestled for four years with the Royals, losing only two matches his senior year and reaching the state final. He was a CIF champion as a junior and a senior.
In the classroom, he compiled a 4.2 GPA and an 1180 SAT score.

Considered a two-star recruit by [[Rivals.com]], Mack chose California over [[Northwestern University|Northwestern]] and [[Stanford University|Stanford]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Alex Mack Profile | url=https://footballrecruiting.rivals.com/viewprospect.asp?pr_key=20346 | work=Rivals.com | access-date=April 22, 2014 | archive-date=May 10, 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200510225454/https://n.rivals.com/ | url-status=dead }}</ref>

==College career==
[[Image:Alex Mack at 2008 Emerald Bowl.JPG|thumb|left|150px|Mack at the [[2008 Emerald Bowl]]]]

Mack played for the [[California Golden Bears football]] team while attending the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/alex-mack-1.html |title=Alex Mack College Stats |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en |access-date=January 7, 2018}}</ref> He made 39 consecutive starts for the Golden Bears  registering 256 key blocks/knockdowns, 32 touchdown-resulting blocks and 29 down field blocks. Mack compiled a 3.61 undergraduate [[GPA]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] as a legal studies major. He graduated in 2008 and played the [[2008 California Golden Bears football team|2008 season]] as a graduate student in education.<ref name="Cal bio">{{cite web |url=http://www.calbears.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/mack_alex03.html |title=Player Bio: Alex Mack - the University of California Official Athletic Site |access-date=April 27, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101226001314/http://www.calbears.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/mack_alex03.html |archive-date=December 26, 2010 }} Cal profile</ref> He won the [[Draddy Trophy]], also dubbed the "academic Heisman", for his academic success in 2008, becoming the first Cal player and the second consecutive center to earn the trophy, following Dallas Griffin of [[Texas Longhorns football|Texas]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.google.com/hostednews/ap/article/ALeqM5hAUa8AMs6H0f5L3jZS7IZWDQzQlwD94VI7CG8|title=Mack wins Draddy as top scholar-athlete}}{{dead link|date=June 2024|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> He also won the [[Morris Trophy]] in 2007 and 2008, making him the third offensive lineman and the first since [[Washington Huskies football|Washington's]] [[Lincoln Kennedy]] in 1991 and 1992 to win the award twice.<ref>{{cite web
 |url=http://www.pac-10.org/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/121708aal.html 
 |title=California's Mack and Oregon's Reed win 29th annual Morris Trophy 
 |publisher=CBS Interactive 
 |access-date=December 18, 2010 |url-status=dead 
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090429184439/http://www.pac-10.org/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/121708aal.html 
 |archive-date=April 29, 2009 }}</ref> Mack also represented Cal at the [[2009 Senior Bowl]].

Projected as a first-to-second rounder by ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'', Mack was the highest ranked center available in the [[2009 NFL draft]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/2009/draft/players/13013.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090426114102/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/2009/draft/players/13013.html|archive-date=April 26, 2009|title=Alex Mack - 2009 Draft Tracker}}</ref>

===Cleveland Browns===
Mack was drafted in the first round by the [[Cleveland Browns]] with the 21st overall selection.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2009 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2009/draft.htm |access-date=May 12, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> He was the first Golden Bears offensive lineman selected in the first round since [[Tarik Glenn]] in [[1997 NFL draft|1997]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/schools/california/drafted.htm |title=California Drafted Players/Alumni |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |access-date=January 7, 2018}}</ref>

Mack signed a five-year contract with the Browns on July 25. During the [[2009 NFL season]], Mack started on the Browns offensive line every game.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/cle/2009_roster.htm |title=2009 Cleveland Browns Starters, Roster, & Players |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |access-date=January 7, 2018}}</ref> After a shaky start, the Browns line, anchored by Joe Thomas, paved the way to three consecutive 100+ yard games by [[Jerome Harrison]] and one game in which Harrison ran for 286 yards, which stands at third all-time in one game.  At the end of the regular season, Mack was selected as center on the All-Rookie team.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.calbears.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/012010aab.html |title=Former Golden Bears DeSean Jackson and Alex Mack Honored by Pro Football Weekly/PFWA |date=January 20, 2010 |access-date=January 20, 2010 |publisher=CBS Interactive |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120307122701/http://www.calbears.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/012010aab.html |archive-date=March 7, 2012 }}</ref> He started all 16 games, committed only 1 penalty and allowed just 1 sack.
[[File:Cleveland Browns Military Appreciation Day DVIDS1098975.jpg|thumb|right|200px|Mack with the Browns in [[2010 Cleveland Browns season|2010]]]]
During the [[2010 NFL season]], Mack again started every game for the Browns.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/cle/2010_roster.htm |title=2010 Cleveland Browns Starters, Roster, & Players |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |access-date=January 7, 2018}}</ref> He was named to the [[2011 Pro Bowl]] roster as a second alternate to replace [[Nick Mangold]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.clevelandbrowns.com/news/article-1/Mack-added-to-Pro-Bowl-roster/b21442b8-7e36-4057-8029-397651e0df5f|title=Mack added to Pro Bowl roster|date=January 4, 2011|access-date=January 4, 2011|publisher=Cleveland Brownsl|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110213182426/http://www.clevelandbrowns.com/news/article-1/Mack-added-to-Pro-Bowl-roster/b21442b8-7e36-4057-8029-397651e0df5f|archive-date=February 13, 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref> During week 5 of the [[2011 NFL season]], Mack played through [[appendicitis]] during a loss to the [[Tennessee Titans]]. Mack had an appendectomy during Cleveland's bye week and came back and started against the [[Oakland Raiders]] the week after the bye week.

On December 27, 2013, Alex Mack was voted to his first [[Pro Bowl]] Selection, after having been added in 2011 to replace an injured player.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2013 NFL Pro Bowlers |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2013/probowl.htm |access-date=2024-12-26 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

On April 9, 2014, it was announced that the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] had offered Mack a five-year contract, worth reportedly $42 million.<ref>{{cite web|last=Schefter|first=Adam|title=Browns transition-tagged center Alex Mack signed his five-year, $42M offer sheet that includes $26M guaranteed with the Jaguars.|url=https://twitter.com/AdamSchefter/status/454658527228088320|publisher=Twitter|access-date=April 11, 2014}}</ref>  The Browns had a maximum of five days to match Jacksonville's offer, which they did on April 11.<ref>{{cite web|title=Cleveland Browns Roster|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/team/roster/_/name/cle/cleveland-browns|publisher=ESPN|access-date=April 9, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Shefter|first=Adam|title=Alex Mack to sign Jags' offer sheet|date=April 9, 2014|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/10757473/alex-mack-sign-offer-sheet-jacksonville-jaguars|publisher=ESPN|access-date=April 9, 2014}}</ref> Mack had been previously assigned the transition tag, nullifying his free agency unless a team signed Mack to an offer sheet. During Week 6 against the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] on October 12, 2014, Mack was carted off the field due to a leg injury. X-rays tested positive that his leg had a broken fibula, forcing Mack out for the rest of the 2014 campaign. Prior to Mack's injury, he had never missed a single snap in his professional career. On  March 2, 2016, Mack voided his contract with the [[Cleveland Browns]] thus making him a free agent.<ref name="u581">{{cite web | last=McManamon | first=Pat | title=Browns' Mack opts out but may return to team | website=ESPN.com | date=2016-03-02 | url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/14884993/cleveland-browns-alex-mack-opting-contract | access-date=2024-10-21}}</ref>

===Atlanta Falcons===
[[File:Atlanta Falcons (45674483812).jpg|thumb|Mack and his teammates in a game against the [[Washington Redskins]] ]]
On March 9, 2016, Mack signed a five-year, $45 million contract with the [[Atlanta Falcons]], including $28.5 million in guaranteed money.<ref name="e950">{{cite web | last=Choate | first=Dave | title=Falcons land #elite center Alex Mack | website=The Falcoholic | date=2016-03-09 | url=https://www.thefalcoholic.com/2016/3/9/11161756/atlanta-falcons-sign-alex-mack-free-agency-2016 | access-date=2024-12-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.spotrac.com/nfl/atlanta-falcons/alex-mack/|title=Alex Mack|last=Spotrac.com|website=Spotrac.com|access-date=March 10, 2016}}</ref>

In the 2016 season, Mack and the Falcons reached [[Super Bowl LI]], where they faced the [[2016 New England Patriots season|New England Patriots]]. Mack was the starting center in the game for the Falcons. In the Super Bowl, the Falcons fell in a 34–28 overtime defeat.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201702050atl.htm|title=Super Bowl LI - New England Patriots vs. Atlanta Falcons - February 5th, 2017|work=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]]|access-date=August 6, 2017}}</ref>

On December 19, 2017, Mack was named to his fifth Pro Bowl.<ref>{{cite web|title=NFL announces 2018 Pro Bowl rosters|url=https://www.nfl.com/news/updated-player-rosters-for-2018-pro-bowl-in-orlando-0ap3000000895772|website=NFL.com|date=December 19, 2017|access-date=December 26, 2017}}</ref> On December 18, 2018, Mack was named to his sixth Pro Bowl.<ref name="y213">{{cite web | title=NFL reveals rosters for 2019 Pro Bowl in Orlando | website=NFL.com | date=2018-12-18 | url=https://www.nfl.com/news/nfl-reveals-rosters-for-2019-pro-bowl-in-orlando-0ap3000001001792 | access-date=2024-12-26}}</ref>

Mack missed Week 16 of the [[2020 NFL season]] due to a [[concussion]], ending a streak of 90 consecutive regular season starts.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Curtis|first=Jake|date=|title=Cal in NFL: Aaron Rodgers Closes Gap in MVP Race With Patrick Mahomes|url=https://www.si.com/college/cal/news/mvp-rodgers-mahomes-week-16|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201228050940/https://www.si.com/college/cal/news/mvp-rodgers-mahomes-week-16 |archive-date=December 28, 2020 |access-date=December 28, 2020|website=Sports Illustrated Cal Bears News|language=en}}</ref> He was placed on the reserve/[[COVID-19]] list by the team on December 31, 2020,<ref>{{cite news |author=McFadden, Will |title=Falcons place Alex Mack on reserve/COVID-19 list |url=https://www.atlantafalcons.com/news/falcons-place-alex-mack-on-reserve-covid-19-list |website=AtlantaFalcons.com |date=December 31, 2020 |access-date=February 11, 2021 |archive-date=January 27, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210127140405/https://www.atlantafalcons.com/news/falcons-place-alex-mack-on-reserve-covid-19-list |url-status=dead }}</ref> and activated on January 13, 2021.<ref>{{cite news |title=Falcons' Alex Mack: Activated from COVID list |url=https://www.cbssports.com/fantasy/football/news/falcons-alex-mack-activated-from-covid-list/ |website=CBSSports.com |date=January 13, 2021 |access-date=February 11, 2021}}</ref>

===San Francisco 49ers===
On March 18, 2021, Mack signed a three-year contract with the [[San Francisco 49ers]].<ref>{{cite web|title=San Francisco 49ers sign Pro Bowl center Alex Mack to 3-year deal|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/31089541/san-francisco-49ers-sign-pro-bowl-center-alex-mack-3-year-deal|author=Wagoner, Nick|website=ESPN.com|date=March 18, 2021}}</ref>

On June 3, 2022, Mack retired after 13 seasons in the NFL.<ref>{{cite web|title=Alex Mack Announces Retirement|url=https://www.49ers.com/news/alex-mack-announces-retirement-nfl-center-49ers-falcons|publisher=49ers.com|date=June 3, 2022|access-date=June 4, 2022|archive-date=June 8, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220608030834/https://www.49ers.com/news/alex-mack-announces-retirement-nfl-center-49ers-falcons|url-status=dead}}</ref>

'''Alex Benjamin Barron''' (born September 28, 1982) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[St. Louis Rams]] with the 19th overall pick of the [[2005 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for [[Florida State University]], and was a two-time consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]].

==Early life==
Barron was born in [[Orangeburg, South Carolina]].  He attended [[Orangeburg-Wilkinson Senior High School|Orangeburg-Wilkinson High School]], and was a two-sport standout in [[high school football|football]] and [[basketball]] for the O-W Bruins.

In football, he was named a high school All-American by both PrepStar and ''Football News'', ranked the No. 3 lineman in the nation by PrepStar, named to the All-South team by the ''[[Orlando Sentinel]]'', and selected as Jeff Whittaker's Deep South Recruiting Guide South Carolina Player of the Year.

==College career==
Barron accepted a football scholarship from [[Florida State University]], where he played for coach [[Bobby Bowden]]'s [[Florida State Seminoles football]] team from 2001 to 2004. As a [[Redshirt (college sports)|redshirt]] freshman, he played in 4 games as a backup. As a sophomore, he appeared in 14 with five starts. As a junior, he started 12 games.

As a senior, he started all 13 games, allowing only five quarterback pressures and one sack, while contributing to the Seminoles gaining 4,470 offensive yards. He was also one of three finalists for the [[Outland Trophy]].

Barron started 30 out of 43 career games at [[left tackle]]. He was a first-team [[List of All-Atlantic Coast Conference football teams|All-Atlantic Coast Conference]] (ACC) selection in 2003 and 2004, and was recognized as a consensus first-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] in 2003 and a unanimous first-team All-American in 2004.<ref>''2011 NCAA Football Records Book'', [http://fs.ncaa.org/Docs/stats/football_records/2011/Awards.pdf  Award Winners], National Collegiate Athletic Association, Indianapolis, Indiana, p. 11 (2011).  Retrieved June 26, 2012.</ref> He graduated from Florida State with a [[bachelor's degree]] in social science.

In 2016, he was inducted into the Florida State University Athletics Hall of Fame. He also has a permanent display in the Seminoles' locker room.

==Professional career==

===St. Louis Rams===
Barron was selected by the [[St. Louis Rams]] in the first round (19th overall) of the [[2005 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2005 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2005/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> On August 14, [[2005 NFL season|2005]], he signed a five-year, $9.2 million contract with the Rams with escalators that could take the value to over $11 million. The contract featured $5.5 million in guaranteed money, not including the signing bonus of $1 million. As a rookie, he was moved to [[right tackle]], because the team had [[All-Pro]] [[Orlando Pace]] starting at [[left tackle]]. Barron passed [[Rex Tucker (American football)|Rex Tucker]] on the depth chart, starting 11 games, while making his pro debut against the [[Tennessee Titans]] and his first start against the [[New York Giants]].

In [[2007 NFL season|2007]], he started 16 games at [[right tackle]]. He switched from right to [[left tackle]] against the [[San Francisco 49ers]], after Pace was injured in Week 1.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3013232 | title=Rams lose offensive line anchor Pace for season | date=September 10, 2007 | access-date=February 19, 2020}}</ref>

In [[2008 NFL season|2008]], he started 15 of 16 games at [[right tackle]], while contributing to [[running back]] [[Steven Jackson]] leading the league with an average of 118.4 yards from scrimmage. He was a part of an offensive line that allowed 45 sacks, the fewest by the Rams since 2003.

In [[2009 NFL season|2009]], he started 16 games at [[left tackle]] after Pace was released. He allowed 7 sacks and led the league with 7 holding penalties. In a 35–0 loss against the [[San Francisco 49ers]], his poor play resulted in him being benched for the rest of the game, after getting an illegal formation penalty for lining up in the backfield.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.stltoday.com/sports/spagnuolo-gives-barron-clean-slate-after-benching-pro-football/article_442ecb95-e406-597c-a83b-244be4b5fdfd.html | title=Spagnuolo gives Barron 'clean slate' after benching | date=October 6, 2009 | access-date=February 19, 2020}}</ref> He contributed to Jackson rushing for more than 1,400 yards (most in the NFC).

In [[2010 NFL season|2010]], the Rams drafted [[offensive tackle]] [[Rodger Saffold]] to compete with Barron. On May 10, he was traded to the [[Dallas Cowboys]], in exchange for another underwhelming former first round draft choice in [[linebacker]] [[Bobby Carpenter (American football)|Bobby Carpenter]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=5177715 |title=Cowboys, Rams swap underachievers |work=ESPN.com |date=May 10, 2010 |access-date=February 19, 2020}}</ref>

Barron had a disappointing career with the Rams, becoming notorious for his inconsistency, false starts and holding penalties. Although he was durable, starting 74 games at both left and right tackle, he struggled with penalties and poor blocking. He committed 43 false start penalties (13 in 2006), 13 holding penalties and allowed 33 sacks.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.stltoday.com/sports/football/nfl-notes-alex-barron-resurfaces-with-raiders/article_37d614af-1e2e-5e6a-80ff-1218cbfb2604.html | title=Alex Barron resurfaces with Raiders | date=August 15, 2013 | access-date=February 19, 2020}}</ref> Such poor play after having been a first round draft has led to him being labeled as a bust among Ram fans.

===Dallas Cowboys===
[[File:Alex Barron cropped.jpg|thumb|200px|Barron with the Cowboys in 2011]]
In [[2010 NFL season|2010]], he was acquired to provide depth and compete with [[Doug Free]] for the left tackle position, after the release of [[Flozell Adams]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.espn.com/dallas/nfl/columns/story?columnist=macmahon_tim&id=5196407 | title=Free welcomes challenge from Barron | date=May 17, 2010 | access-date=February 19, 2020}}</ref> He got off to an inauspicious beginning, in his first game and start at [[right tackle]] in place of an injured [[Marc Colombo]], the Cowboys appeared to have come back from a 13–7 deficit on a [[touchdown]] pass from [[Tony Romo]] to [[Roy Williams (wide receiver)|Roy Williams]] on the final play against the [[Washington Redskins]] on the season opener.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.espn.com/blog/dallas/cowboys/post/_/id/4671781/injury-update-colombo-and-kosier-in-question | title=Injuries: Colombo and Kosier in question | date=September 6, 2010 | access-date=February 19, 2020}}</ref> However, Barron was flagged for holding [[defensive end]] [[Brian Orakpo]] and because the penalty was called against the offense, the game was over with the Cowboys losing.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.espn.com/dallas/nfl/news/story?id=5569113 | title=Alex Barron apologizes to Roy Williams | date=September 13, 2010 | access-date=February 19, 2020}}</ref> Although he was active for 10 additional games, he would not play another down and was not re-signed at the end of the year.

===New Orleans Saints===
On August 3, [[2011 NFL season|2011]], Barron signed with the [[New Orleans Saints]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.espn.com/blog/nflnation/post/_/id/42829/saints-take-a-shot-on-two-tackles?redirected=true | title=Saints take a shot on two tackles | date=August 3, 2011 | access-date=February 19, 2020}}</ref> On August 18, he was put on the [[injured reserve list]]. He was waived with an injury settlement on October 22.

===Seattle Seahawks===
On May 15, [[2012 NFL season|2012]], he signed as a [[free agent]] with the [[Seattle Seahawks]], after having a tryout with the team during rookie minicamp.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/7935213/seattle-seahawks-former-first-round-pick-alex-barron-agree-deal | title=Seahawks, Alex Barron agree to deal | work=ESPN | date=May 16, 2012 | access-date=February 19, 2020}}</ref> He was cut on August 26.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story?id=8304677&src=desktop | title=T.O. released by Seahawks | work=ESPN | date=August 26, 2012 | access-date=February 19, 2020}}</ref>

===Oakland Raiders===
On March 26, [[2013 NFL season|2013]], Barron signed with the [[Oakland Raiders]], to provide depth after starter [[Jared Veldheer]] suffered a torn left triceps.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.raiders.com/news/article-1/Raiders-Add-Former-First-Round-Selection-Alex-Barron/0a047d99-0885-4971-9891-24e1f356d664 |title=Raiders Add Former First-Round Selection Alex Barron |access-date=March 26, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130329013541/http://www.raiders.com/news/article-1/Raiders-Add-Former-First-Round-Selection-Alex-Barron/0a047d99-0885-4971-9891-24e1f356d664 |archive-date=March 29, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref> On September 2, he was released to make room on the roster for [[offensive tackle]] [[Tony Pashos]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.espn.com/blog/afcwest/post/_/id/61721/raiders-add-more-o-line-depth | title=Raiders add more O-line depth | work=ESPN | date=September 2, 2013 | access-date=February 19, 2020}}</ref>

'''Alex James Brown''' (born June 4, 1979) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for nine seasons. He played [[college football]] for the [[Florida Gators football|Florida Gators]], and was a two-time [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]]. The [[Chicago Bears]] picked Brown in the fourth round of the [[2002 NFL draft]], and he also played for the [[New Orleans Saints]].

== Early life ==

Brown was born in [[Jasper, Florida]] in 1979.<ref name="nflprofile">National Football League, Historical Players, [http://www.nfl.com/player/alexbrown/2505098/profile  Alex Brown].  Retrieved March 17, 2012.</ref>  He attended Hamilton County High School in Jasper,<ref name="dbfprofile">databaseFootball.com, Players, {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20110528123147/http://databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=BROWNALE01  Alex Brown]}}. Alex attended South Hamilton Elementary school. Alex played football and basketball under coach Chuck Fultz.  Retrieved March 16, 2011.</ref> and played high school football for the Hamilton County Trojans.<ref name="ufprofile">GatorZone.com, Football History, 2001 Roster, [http://web.gatorzone.com/football/bios.php?year=2001&bio=brown.html  Alex Brown] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111006162547/http://web.gatorzone.com/football/bios.php?year=2001&bio=brown.html |date=October 6, 2011 }}.  Retrieved March 24, 2011.</ref>  As the Trojans' senior quarterback in 1996, Brown threw for 863 yards and four touchdowns, and rushed for 767 yards and eighteen touchdowns; as a starting linebacker, he also compiled 117 total tackles (with seven tackles for loss), five blocked passes, four fumble recoveries, two forced fumbles and two blocked field goals.<ref name=ufprofile/>  He was honored as a Florida Class 3A all-state selection and a National Recruiting Adviser and SuperPrep high school All-American.<ref name=ufprofile/>  Brown was also a standout basketball player and track and field athlete, and was the state champion discus thrower in 1996.<ref name=ufprofile/>

== College career ==

Brown accepted an athletic scholarship to attend the [[University of Florida]] in Gainesville, Florida, where he played for coach [[Steve Spurrier]]'s [[Florida Gators football]] team from [[1998 Florida Gators football team|1998]] to [[2001 Florida Gators football team|2001]].<ref name="ufmediaguide">''[http://web.gatorzone.com/football/media/2012/media_guide.pdf  2012 Florida Football Media Guide] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130527130648/http://web.gatorzone.com/football/media/2012/media_guide.pdf |date=May 27, 2013 }}'', University Athletic Association, Gainesville, Florida, pp. 77, 84, 88, 89, 92, 93, 95, 97, 100, 104, 116, 158, 176, 185 (2012).  Retrieved September 15, 2012.</ref>  The Gators coaching staff decided to [[redshirt (college sports)|red-shirt]] him as a true freshman in [[1997 Florida Gators football team|1997]].<ref name=ufprofile/>  He saw action at [[outside linebacker]] in [[1998 Florida Gators football team|1998]], recording ten tackles with two sacks and three tackles for a loss as the backup to All-American starter [[Jevon Kearse]].<ref name=ufprofile/>

As a sophomore starter in [[1999 Florida Gators football team|1999]], Brown recorded fifty-six tackles with 7.5 sacks and twelve tackles for a loss.<ref name=ufprofile/>  Arguably, he played his best college game on September 18, 1999, when he sacked [[quarterback]] [[Tee Martin]] five times in the Gators' 23–21 upset of the second-ranked [[1999 Tennessee Volunteers football team|Tennessee Volunteers]].<ref name=ufprofile/>  He was honored as first-team [[List of All-SEC football teams|All-Southeastern Conference]] (SEC) selection and first-team [[1999 College Football All-America Team|All-American]] by the [[Walter Camp Foundation]] and ''Football News'', and was one of the twelve semi-finalists for the [[Lombardi Award]].<ref name=ufmediaguide/>

During the Gators' [[2000 Florida Gators football team|2000]] SEC championship season, Brown was a team captain and started every game at right defensive end, recording fifty tackles with 10.5 sacks, fourteen tackles for a loss and four blocked passes, while forcing a fumble and blocking three kicks.<ref name=ufprofile/><ref name=ufmediaguide/>  Brown was a first-team All-SEC selection, a second-team [[2000 College Football All-America Team|All-American]], and was once again one of the twelve semi-finalists for the Lombardi Award.<ref name=ufmediaguide/>

As a senior in [[2001 Florida Gators football team|2001]], Brown recorded forty-five tackles and a career-best thirteen sacks.<ref name=ufprofile/>  He was a first-team All-SEC selection, and was recognized as a consensus first-team [[2001 College Football All-America Team|All-American]], after receiving first-team honors from a majority of All-American selector organizations.<ref name=ufmediaguide/><ref>''2012 NCAA Football Records Book'', [http://fs.ncaa.org/Docs/stats/football_records/2012/Awards.pdf  Award Winners], National Collegiate Athletic Association, Indianapolis, Indiana, pp. 11 & 14 (2012).  Retrieved September 14, 2012.</ref>  He was also the 2001 SEC Defensive Player of the Year, one of the four finalists for the Lombardi Award, and one of five finalists of the [[Bronko Nagurski Trophy]].<ref name=ufmediaguide/>

During his four-year college career, Brown totaled 161 tackles with forty-seven tackles for a loss (sixth-best career total in Gators history), and set the Gators' current career record of thirty-three quarterback sacks.<ref name=ufmediaguide/>  He was inducted into the [[List of University of Florida Athletic Hall of Fame members|University of Florida Athletic Hall of Fame]] as a "Gator Great" in 2012.<ref>F Club, Hall of Fame, [http://www.gatorfclub.org/hall-of-fame/greats  Gator Greats].  Retrieved December 13, 2014.</ref><ref>"[http://www.gatorzone.com/story.php?id=21249  Florida Announces 2012 UF Athletic Hall of Fame Inductees] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131019081452/http://www.gatorzone.com/story.php?id=21249 |date=2013-10-19 }}," GatorZone.com (September 7, 2011).  Retrieved September 24, 2011.</ref>

=== Chicago Bears ===

The Chicago Bears selected Brown in the fourth round (104th pick overall) of the [[2002 NFL draft]],<ref>Pro Football Hall of Fame, Draft History, [http://www.profootballhof.com/history/story.aspx?story_id=2039  2002 National Football League Draft] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121002215045/http://www.profootballhof.com/history/story.aspx?story_id=2039 |date=October 2, 2012 }}.  Retrieved March 17, 2012.</ref> and he played for the Bears from {{NFL Year|2002}} to {{NFL Year|2009}}.<ref name=nflprofile/><ref>{{Cite web |title=2002 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2002/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-18 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>  As a rookie, he started nine of the fifteen games in which he played at right defensive end and logged 2.5 quarterback sacks.<ref name="pfrprofile">{{Cite web |title=Alex Brown Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BrowAl20.htm |access-date=2025-05-11 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>  He also totaled 40 tackles (31 unassisted) and three passes broken up, while also contributing on special teams coverage.<ref name=pfrprofile/>  During the {{NFL Year|2003}} season, his first as a full-time starter, he led the Bears with 5.5 sacks, with a career-high fifty-eight tackles (forty-nine solos), and six tackles for losses while forcing two fumbles and recovering a fumble.<ref name=nflprofile/>

He started at right defensive end for all sixteen regular season games in {{NFL Year|2004}}, and compiling six sacks and fifty tackles, with eleven tackles for a loss and nine passes defensed.<ref name=pfrprofile/>  In a game against the [[New York Giants]] on November 7, 2004, Brown recorded a career-high four sacks to go along with eight tackles, including six solos stops.  He also forced a fumble and batted down a pass at the line of scrimmage.  For his efforts, Brown was named the NFL Defensive Player of the Week by ''[[Pro Football Weekly]]''.

[[File:Bears-def-huddle-2008.jpg|thumb|275px|left|Brown, along with [[Adewale Ogunleye]], [[Tommie Harris]] and [[Mark Anderson (American football)|Mark Anderson]] during training camp in 2008.]]

Brown was a first-alternate for the Pro Bowl after recording 75 tackles (nine for a loss) and six sacks, eight broken up passes and three forced fumbles during the {{NFL Year|2005}} season.<ref name=nflprofile/>  ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' selected him for its All-Pro Team.  He was named NFC Defensive Player of the Week following the game against the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] on November 27, 2005.  In 2006, he was selected as a second-alternate for the Pro Bowl after recording a career-high seven sacks and two interceptions while making forty-six tackles, three forced fumbles, two fumble recoveries and two passes broken up while starting all sixteen games at right defensive end.<ref name=nflprofile/>

In {{NFL Year|2007}} Brown tied for the team lead with five passes broken up, tied for second with five tackles for a loss and two fumble recoveries and tied for third with two forced fumbles, after playing in all sixteen games (two starts) for the fifth straight year, extending his consecutive games played streak to a team-high ninety-five contests.  He ranked second on the defensive line with fifty-eight tackles and added five quarterback hits, 4.5 sacks, one interception, two forced fumbles and a blocked kick.

On December 22, 2008, Brown deflected a [[Field goal (football)|field goal]] attempt by Packers kicker [[Mason Crosby]] in the final twenty-five seconds of the fourth quarter to set up the game-winning field goal for the Bears in a 20–17 overtime victory over the [[Green Bay Packers]].  In the second game of the {{NFL Year|2009}} season, the Bears upset the defending Super Bowl champion Pittsburgh Steelers 17–14, and Brown recorded two key sacks of Steelers quarterback [[Ben Roethlisberger]].  Brown was later carted off the field with four minutes left in the game with a sprained ankle.

After the 2009 season, the Bears released Brown on April 1, 2010, after failing to trade him to another team.<ref>Larry Mayer, "[http://www.chicagobears.com/news/NewsStory.asp?story_id=6658  Bears release veteran defensive end Alex Brown] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100403000615/http://www.chicagobears.com/news/NewsStory.asp?story_id=6658 |date=April 3, 2010 }}," Chicago Bears (April 1, 2010).  Retrieved March 24, 2011.</ref>

=== New Orleans Saints ===
On April 7, 2010, the [[New Orleans Saints]] signed Brown to a two-year contract.<ref>Nakia Hogan, "[http://www.nola.com/saints/index.ssf/2010/04/free_agent_defensive_end_alex.html Free agent defensive end Alex Brown signs with the New Orleans Saints]," ''The Times-Picayune'' (April 7, 2010).  Retrieved March 24, 2011.</ref>  He played his final NFL season for the Saints, starting in all sixteen games at left defensive end.<ref name=nflprofile/> The Saints released Brown on August 30, 2011.

=== Retirement ===

On August 9, 2012, Alex Brown signed a one-day contract with the Bears to officially retire with the team.  With the Bears, his 43.5 sacks rank fourth in team history, and his five interceptions rank second behind [[Richard Dent]] among Bears defensive ends.<ref name="ChicagoBears">http://www.chicagobears.com/news/NewsStory.asp?story_id=8961{{Dead link|date=September 2019 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

In his nine-season NFL career, Brown played in 143 regular season games, started 123 of them, and compiled 421 tackles, 43.5 quarterback sacks, forty-two deflected passes, seventeen forced fumbles with twelve recovered, and five interceptions.<ref name=pfrprofile/>

== Life after football ==
Brown works for Coyote Logistics.

Brown is an analyst for the 120 Sports "Football Fix" in Chicago. He, former Bears teammate [[Desmond Clark]], and "non-descript white guy" Ryan Steele also host the ''Dez Clark & Alex Brown Show'' sports radio talk show in Chicago.<ref>[http://www.dezclarkshow.com/  The Dez Clark & Alex Brown Show] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120128180200/http://www.dezclarkshow.com/ |date=January 28, 2012 }}.  Retrieved March 17, 2012.</ref><ref>"[http://www.dailyherald.com/article/20120117/submitted/120119875/  Tilted Kilt hosts Dez Clark & Alex Brown Show Jan. 19]," ''Daily Herald'' (January 17, 2012).  Retrieved March 17, 2012.</ref> Following Bears games, Brown, [[David Kaplan (radio)|David Kaplan]], former teammate [[Lance Briggs]], and former Bears head coach Dave Wannstedt serve as analysts for [[NBC Sports Chicago]]'s ''Football Aftershow''.<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 20, 2019 |title=Olin Kreutz to join NBC Sports Chicago's Bears coverage team |url=https://www.nbcsports.com/chicago/bears/olin-kreutz-join-nbc-sports-chicagos-bears-coverage-team |website=[[NBC Sports Chicago]] |accessdate=August 20, 2019}}</ref>

He is a [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] precinct committeeman in [[Vernon Hills, Illinois]] where he resides with his wife, Kari, who serves as a village trustee.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kambic |first=Rick |title=Vernon Hills appoints County Board candidate to vacant trustee seat |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/suburbs/vernon-hills/news/ct-vhr-karimar-brown-vernon-hills-appointment-tl-0920-story.html |access-date=January 8, 2019 |website=chicagotribune.com |date=September 14, 2018 |language=en-US}}</ref>

'''Alex M. Molden''' (born August 4, 1973) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Oregon Ducks football|Oregon Ducks]] and was selected by the [[New Orleans Saints]] in the first round with the 11th overall pick of the [[1996 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1996 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1996/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-30 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>  He played between 1996 and 2004 for the [[New Orleans Saints]], the [[San Diego Chargers]] and the [[Detroit Lions]].<ref>[http://www.nfl.com/player/alexmolden/2502162/profile NFL profile]</ref>

==College career==
Molden played [[college football]] at the [[University of Oregon]] and was on the team that reached the [[1994 Oregon Ducks football team|1995]] [[Rose Bowl (game)|Rose Bowl]]. He was redshirted in 1991. In 1992 he had 55 tackles, four interceptions, and 19 passes broken up. He suffered a devastating knee injury in the Independence Bowl, and tore his anterior cruciate, medial collateral and posterior cruciate ligaments. He came back after a nine-month rehabilitation to start nine games in 1993. He was selected as an All-Pacific 10 cornerback in 1994, and was an All-Pacific 10/Football Coaches Association All-American and Associated Press second-team All-American in 1995.

'''Alex Brink''' (born June 2, 1985) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] [[quarterback]]. After playing [[college football]] at [[Washington State Cougars football|Washington State]], Brink was selected by the [[Houston Texans]] in the seventh round of the [[2008 NFL draft]].

In 2010, he joined the [[Winnipeg Blue Bombers]] of the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL). Brink was also a member of the [[Toronto Argonauts]] and [[Montreal Alouettes]].

==Early life==
A native of Eugene, Oregon,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Larson Jr. |first=Craig |date=2024-12-24 |title=Former Washington State star quarterback shares thoughts on John Mateer |url=https://athlonsports.com/college/oklahoma-sooners/former-washington-state-star-quarterback-shares-thoughts-on-john-mateer |access-date=2025-04-23 |website=Athlon Sports |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=October 10, 2007 |title=Race in football: WSU QB Alex Brink doesn't mince words |url=https://247sports.com/article/race-in-football-wsu-qb-alex-brink-doesnt-mince-words-104459243/ |access-date=2025-04-23 |website=247Sports |language=en}}</ref> Brink attended [[Sheldon High School (Eugene, Oregon)|Sheldon High School]], and becoming a [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] in [[High school football|football]], [[basketball]] and [[baseball]]. In football, as a senior, he led his team to the state championship, with a 31–24 win over [[Lake Oswego High School|Lake Oswego]]. During that season he [[Passing (American football)#Advancing the ball|passed]] for 3946 yards and 36 [[touchdown]]s, while being named Oregon Player of the Year. He passed for over 3,500 yards in his junior season as well. His record as a high school [[Starting lineup|starter]] was 35–3, with one state championship. In baseball, he was a standout player and threw a [[Perfect game (baseball)|perfect game]]. He graduated from Sheldon High in 2003 with a 3.91 [[Grading in education|GPA]].

==College career==

Brink finished his career as one of Washington State's all-time greats, holding the school career records in passing yards, touchdowns, attempts, completions and total offense. His senior year, he threw for 3,818 yards, the second highest single-season total in school's history. He is the only Cougar to have five 400-plus yard games and has five of the top 10 and three of the top four passing games in WSU history.  Although the program was coming off three consecutive 10 win seasons when Brink inherited the team, he failed to lead the Cougars to a single winning season in four years as a starter.

Brink finished his career as the third leading passer, in terms of yards, in [[Pacific-10 Conference|Pac-10]] history, behind [[Carson Palmer]] and [[Derek Anderson (American football)|Derek Anderson]] and fifth leader in touchdowns. He is also only the sixth signal caller in conference history to throw for more than 10,000 yards and toss 70-or-more touchdowns. In his [[College football|college career]], Brink completed 58.4 percent of his passes for 10,913 yards. He threw 76 touchdowns but also 43 [[interceptions]]. Brink led the Cougars to four straight seasons without a [[Bowl game|bowl]] berth. As a starter, Brink was 17–23 over four seasons. 
 
During a game against [[Oregon State University]] in the 2005 season Brink set a new school record with 531 passing yards. Ahead 30–16 at the break, the Cougars, however, lost that game due in part to [[Defense (sport)|defensive]] and [[special teams]] lapses and other mistakes, but also because Brink threw one touchdown against four interceptions. For much of the 2006 season, Brink led the Pac-10 in passing yards. He was named second-team All-Pac-10 for his efforts. The Cougars were at one point in the 2006 season ranked No. 25 in the nation with a 6–3 record, but lost their final three games to finish the year at 6-6.  In 2006-2007 Pac-10 rankings, he led the league in total offense with 242.2 yards per game, was second in passing at 241.6 ypg, and fourth in passing efficiency.

Brink finished his senior year as the 2007 Pac-10 leader in total offense and named second-team All-Pac-10. His final game as a Cougar resulted in a come-from-behind, 42–35 victory over rival University of Washington in the annual Apple Cup in which he threw for 399 yards and five touchdowns. He remains the only WSU quarterback ever to beat Washington three times.

===Houston Texans===
Brink was selected by the [[Houston Texans]] in the seventh round (223rd overall) of the [[2008 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2008 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2008/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-12 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He signed a rookie contract with the team on June 27, 2008. He was later released on August 29 during final cuts.

The Texans re-signed Brink to the [[practice squad]] on October 8 after [[cornerback]] [[Derrick Roberson]] was released. He was re-signed to a future contract at the end of the year. The Texans waived Brink on June 24, only to re-sign him on August 17 after an injury to [[Rex Grossman]]. He was waived again on September 5.

===Winnipeg Blue Bombers===
Brink tried out for the [[New York Jets]]<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20100430082459/http://www.google.com/hostednews/canadianpress/article/ALeqM5h4x4-WRAIJcxdNSrkDq8fat2yNGg Source: New York Jets sign 10 UFAs, including Michigan CB Donovan Warren]</ref> in late April but shortly after he agreed to a contract with the [[Winnipeg Blue Bombers]] of the CFL for the 2010 season.<ref>[http://www.winnipegsun.com/sports/football/2010/05/02/13801246.html Bombers crowded at QB]</ref>

In early August 2012, he was named the starting quarterback for Winnipeg, following an injury to [[Buck Pierce]].<ref name=Owen>{{cite news|last=Owen|first=Judy|title=Winnipeg's Brink brings a confident vibe|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/sports/football/winnipegs-brink-brings-a-confident-vibe/article4459607/|access-date=3 August 2012|newspaper=[[The Globe and Mail]]|date=3 August 2012|agency=[[Canadian Press]]|location=Winnipeg}}</ref> After a string of poor performances as the starter, he was replaced by [[Joey Elliott]].

Brink was released by the Blue Bombers on April 8, 2013.<ref>[https://www.tsn.ca/cfl/story/?id=420202 BLUE BOMBERS RELEASE QB BRINK]</ref> Brink spent three seasons with the Blue Bombers, starting 7 games over that time. He threw for 2,573 yards with 13 touchdowns and 13 interceptions.

===Toronto Argonauts===
On April 29, 2013, Brink signed with the [[Toronto Argonauts]].<ref>[https://www.tsn.ca/cfl/story/?id=422041 Signs with the Argonauts]</ref> He was released by the Argonauts on May 16, 2013.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://argonauts.ca/article/argonauts-add-pivot-mitchell-gale |title=ARGONAUTS ADD PIVOT MITCHELL GALE | Toronto Argonauts |access-date=2013-05-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130729050709/http://argonauts.ca/article/argonauts-add-pivot-mitchell-gale |archive-date=2013-07-29 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Montreal Alouettes===
On October 3, 2013, Brink signed with the Montreal Alouettes.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://cfl.ca/article/brink-inked-quarterback-joins-als-practice-roster |title=Brink inked: Quarterback joins Als practice roster | CFL.ca | Official Site of the Canadian Football League |access-date=2013-10-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131003231416/http://www.cfl.ca/article/brink-inked-quarterback-joins-als-practice-roster |archive-date=2013-10-03 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He began the [[2014 Montreal Alouettes season|2014 season]] as a back-up to [[Troy Smith]], but after ineffective play by Smith, Brink took over as the team's starting quarterback in week 8. He started two games before he was replaced by [[Jonathan Crompton]], who remained the starter until the conclusion of the season. On February 6, 2015, Brink was released after the team had signed [[John Skelton (American football)|John Skelton]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://cfl.ca/article/als-release-brink-add-qb-john-skelton |title=Als release Brink; add QB John Skelton |access-date=2015-02-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150208015011/http://cfl.ca/article/als-release-brink-add-qb-john-skelton |archive-date=2015-02-08 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

'''Alex Lewis''' (born June 11, 1981) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 2004–08 for the [[Detroit Lions]]. 

== College career ==
Lewis played [[college football]] from 2000–01 with [[SUNY Morrisville]], earning conference player of the year honors in 2001 with a reported 100 tackles and ten sacks,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ironside |first=Lee |title=Football focuses on defense, special teams with new recruiting class |url=https://badgerherald.com/sports/2002/02/07/football-focuses-on/ |access-date=2026-02-26 |website=The Badger Herald}}</ref> before transferring to the [[Wisconsin Badgers football|Wisconsin Badgers]] where he played in 2002–03.

With Wisconsin, Lewis holds the record for most [[tackles for a loss]] in a game with 6.5, which he accumulated on October 18, 2003 vs. [[2003 Purdue Boilermakers football team|Purdue]]. His performance in this game includes five sacks, good for a tie for second-most in program history. A two-year starter joining the Badgers with two years eligibility, Lewis led the Badgers in tackles in [[2002 Wisconsin Badgers football team|2002]], his junior season, and earned [[2003 All-Big Ten Conference football team|All-Big Ten]] First Team honors in [[2003 Wisconsin Badgers football team|2003]], as a senior.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-02-07 |title=2025 FB RecordBook |url=https://uwbadgers.com/documents/2025/8/22/2025_FB_RecordBook.pdf |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=Wisconsin Badgers |language=en}}</ref>

== Professional career ==

Lewis was selected by the [[Detroit Lions]] in the fifth round of the [[2004 NFL draft]] with the 140th overall pick.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2004/draft.htm |title=2004 NFL Draft Listing |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en |access-date=2023-05-06}}</ref>

Lewis had his most statistically prolific season of his NFL career as a rookie in [[2004 Detroit Lions season|2004]], playing in 15 games making 59 tackles (44 solo), two sacks, and an interception as he saw time on the field both defensively and on special teams.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Alex Lewis Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LewiAl20.htm |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Lewis opened the [[2005 Detroit Lions season|2005 season]] as a starting strong-side linebacker, but suffered a season-ending ankle injury during that game, spending the remainder of the season on [[Injured reserve list|injured reserve]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2007-03-01 |title=Lions resign LB Alex Lewis! |url=https://www.si.com/college/michiganstate/hondos-blog/lions-resign-lb-alex-lewis |access-date=2026-02-26 |website=Michigan State Spartans On SI |language=en-US}}</ref> 

Lewis bounced back from injury with 48 tackles (37 solo), forcing the first fumble of his NFL career, in [[2006 Detroit Lions season|2006]], playing 11 games, starting two, for the Lions that year. Following a successful 2006 campaign, Lewis was viewed as a reliable back-up option behind [[Boss Bailey]] at the strong-side LB position for the [[2007 Detroit Lions season|2007 season]], with his speed, recognition skills, and short zone passing coverage hailed as strengths.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kowalski |first=Tom |date=2007-07-10 |title=Scouting Report: Alex Lewis |url=https://www.mlive.com/lionsinsider/2007/07/scouting_report_alex_lewis.html |access-date=2026-02-26 |website=mlive |language=en}}</ref> Lewis made 14 appearances, with one start, in 2007, forcing another fumble, recovering it (for the first time in his NFL career) and making 29 tackles (24 solo). Lewis would play his final year in the NFL for the infamous [[2008 Detroit Lions season|2008 Detroit Lions]], who became the first NFL team in history to finish a season [[List of winless seasons#Gridiron football|0-16]]. Lewis made 11 appearances with four starts, logging 41 tackles (31 solo) and forcing and recovering a fumble.

Lewis would be released by the Lions in July 2009.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Seifert |first=Kevin |date=2009-07-09 |title=Lions ditch another former draft choice |url=https://www.espn.com/blog/nfcnorth/post/_/id/2190/lions-ditch-another-former-draft-choice |access-date=2026-02-26 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref>

'''Alex Haynes''' (born February 13, 1982) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[UCF Knights football|UCF Knights]] and was signed by the [[Baltimore Ravens]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2005.

Haynes also played for the [[Carolina Panthers]], [[Denver Broncos]] and [[Florida Tuskers]].

==Early life==
Haynes attended [[Maynard Evans High School]] in Orlando, Florida and went on to play at the [[University of Central Florida]] from 2000 to 2004.

==Professional career==

===First stint with the Ravens===
Haynes was signed as an undrafted free agent by the [[Baltimore Ravens]] in 2005.

===Carolina Panthers===
After playing in [[NFL Europe]] in 2006, Haynes was signed by the Carolina Panthers.  He was released on September 2 and was signed to the practice squad on September 3. He was re-signed by the Panthers for the 2007 season, but was waived on September 7. He was later re-signed to the practice squad. The Panthers signed him from the practice squad on October 6. The Panthers tendered Haynes as an exclusive rights free agent and he was re-signed on February 26, 2008, to a one-year, $370,000 contract. He was released in late July.

===Second stint with the Ravens===
On August 1, 2008, Haynes signed with the Ravens. He was waived August 30.

===Denver Broncos===
On November 10, 2008, Haynes was signed by the Denver Broncos. He was released on November 22 and re-signed on December 22. He was later released again on February 11, 2009.

===Florida Tuskers===
Haynes was signed by the [[Florida Tuskers]] of the [[United Football League (2009–)|United Football League]] on September 9, 2009.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.oursportscentral.com/services/releases/?id=3903015 |title=UFL's Florida Tuskers Announce Signing of Eight Additional Players|date=September 9, 2009 |work=OurSports Central |accessdate=August 30, 2011}}</ref>

'''Alex Groncier Gordon''' (born September 14, 1964) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1987 through 1993. He played [[college football]] for the [[Cincinnati Bearcats football|Cincinnati Bearcats]]. Gordon was initiated into the [[Omega Psi Phi]] fraternity at Cincinnati, through the Psi Theta chapter.

According to an August 1987 ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' article, [[Chicago Bears]] coach [[Mike Ditka]] wanted to draft Gordon in the first round (No. 26 overall) in the [[1987 NFL draft]]. However, Ditka was overruled by the Bears' front office, which instead selected [[Michigan Wolverines football|Michigan]] quarterback [[Jim Harbaugh]]. The Jets selected Gordon in the second round with the 42nd overall pick that year.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1987 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1987/draft.htm |access-date=2023-09-25 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

In 1995, Gordon began playing in the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL) for the U.S. expansion [[Memphis Mad Dogs]]. In that one season, he led the team with 61 tackles and 7 sacks.

In 1996, after the Mad Dogs folded, he was selected by the [[Toronto Argonauts]] during the dispersal draft.  He went on to win the [[84th Grey Cup]] with the Argonauts that season.

'''Alex Hall''' (born August 17, 1985) is a former professional [[Canadian football]] [[defensive end]]. He was selected by the [[Cleveland Browns]] in the seventh round of the [[2008 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] at [[St. Augustine's University|St. Augustine's College]].

Hall was a member of the [[Philadelphia Eagles]], [[Arizona Cardinals]], [[New York Giants]], and [[Carolina Panthers]] in the [[National Football League]] and the [[Winnipeg Blue Bombers]] and [[Saskatchewan Roughriders]] of the CFL.

==Professional career==

===Cleveland Browns===
Hall was selected by the [[Cleveland Browns]] in the seventh round of the [[2008 NFL draft]] with the 231st overall pick.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2008 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2008/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-12 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He signed a four-year contract with the team on July 22, 2008.<ref>{{cite web |title=Browns sign 5 draft picks to 4-year contracts |url=http://www.foxnews.com/wires/2008Jul22/0,4670,FBNBrownsSignings,00.html |publisher=FOXNews.com |date=July 22, 2008 |access-date=April 2, 2010}}</ref>

===Philadelphia Eagles===
On April 2, 2010, Hall and the 2010 fourth and fifth-round draft picks were traded to the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] in exchange for linebacker [[Chris Gocong]] and [[Sheldon Brown (American football)|Sheldon Brown]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Schefter |first=Adam |author-link=Adam Schefter |date=April 2, 2010 |title=Eagles CB Brown traded to Cleveland |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=5050119 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100406074951/http://sports.espn.go.com/nfl/news/story?id=5050119 |archive-date=April 6, 2010 |access-date=April 2, 2010 |website=[[ESPN.com]]}}</ref> He was waived on July 28, 2010.<ref>{{cite news |author=Wulf, Bo |title=S Allen Signed; LB Hall Released To Make Room |url=http://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/news/Story.asp?story_id=21396 |work=philadelphiaeagles.com |date=July 28, 2010 |access-date=July 28, 2010 }}{{Dead link|date=October 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

===New York Giants===
Hall was claimed off waivers by the [[New York Giants]] on July 29, 2010.<ref>{{cite news |author=Garafolo, Mike |title=Giants claim defensive end Alex Hall off waivers from the Eagles |url=http://www.nj.com/giants/index.ssf/2010/07/giants_claim_defensive_end_ale.html |work=nj.com |date=July 29, 2010 |access-date=July 29, 2010| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100731134002/http://www.nj.com/giants/index.ssf/2010/07/giants_claim_defensive_end_ale.html| archive-date= July 31, 2010 | url-status= live}}</ref> He was waived by the Giants on September 4, 2010.

===Arizona Cardinals===
Hall signed with the [[Arizona Cardinals]] on September 21, 2010. He was waived by the team on October 30.

===New York Giants (second stint)===
Hall was claimed off waivers from the Arizona Cardinals on November 1, 2010, and placed on the active roster, replacing Giants cornerback [[Bruce Johnson (American football)|Bruce Johnson]], who was placed on injured reserve. On November 27, Hall was waived to make room for [[Michael Coe (American football)|Michael Coe]], who was signed to the active roster.<ref name="b827">{{cite web | title=New York Giants Sign Michael Coe to 53-Man Roster, Waive Alex Hall | website=Big Blue Interactive | date=2010-11-28 | url=https://www.bigblueinteractive.com/2010/11/28/giants-jaguars-gameday-roster-moves/ | access-date=2024-11-28}}</ref> While he worked out for the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] on December 14, 2010,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.yardbarker.com/blog/nflbuzz/steelers_work_out_four_players/3796448|title=Yardbarker.com|website=Yardbarker|access-date=December 15, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101218153353/http://www.yardbarker.com/blog/nflbuzz/steelers_work_out_four_players/3796448|archive-date=December 18, 2010|url-status=dead}}</ref> he was re-signed on December 15 after linebacker [[Clint Sintim]] was placed on injured reserve.

===Winnipeg Blue Bombers===
Hall signed with the [[Winnipeg Blue Bombers]] of the Canadian Football League on April 24, 2012. He ended the season as an East Division All-Star and was named Winnipeg's Most Outstanding Defensive Player.

===Saskatchewan Roughriders===
On October 6, 2013, Hall was traded (along with a 2nd-round pick in the [[2014 CFL draft]]) to the [[Saskatchewan Roughriders]] in exchange for non-import lineman [[Patrick Neufeld]] and a 5th round selection in [[2015 CFL draft]]. At the time of the trade, Hall led the league in sacks with 15, by the end of the season he would be 2nd in the league with 16 sacks.<ref>https://www.tsn.ca/cfl/story/?id=433570 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140318003036/http://www.tsn.ca/cfl/story/?id=433570 |date=March 18, 2014 }} Traded to Saskatchewan</ref> Since Hall's CFL contract expired at the end of the [[2013 CFL season]] it was expected that would try out for an NFL team for the following season. Hall also won the [[Grey Cup]] that year.

===Carolina Panthers===
On April 11, 2014, Hall signed with the [[Carolina Panthers]].<ref>{{cite web|work=NFL.com|url=https://www.nfl.com/news/alex-hall-ex-cfl-standout-signs-deal-with-panthers-0ap2000000340934|title=Alex Hall, ex-CFL standout, signs deal with Panthers|first=Dan|last=Hanzus|date=April 11, 2014|access-date=April 12, 2014}}</ref> The Panthers released Hall on August 24, 2014.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Panthers make first wave of cuts |url=http://www.panthers.com/news/article-2/Panthers-make-first-wave-of-cuts/3b95dbb1-bb41-4720-98a3-6e9d8c138701 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140826114055/http://www.panthers.com/news/article-2/Panthers-make-first-wave-of-cuts/3b95dbb1-bb41-4720-98a3-6e9d8c138701 |archive-date=August 26, 2014 |access-date=August 24, 2014 |website=Panthers.com}}</ref>

===Saskatchewan Roughriders (II)===
Hall re-signed with the Roughriders on February 11, 2015.<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 11, 2015 |title=Former all-star DE Alex Hall returns to Riderville |url=https://www.cfl.ca/article/former-all-star-de-alex-hall-returns-to-riderville |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923222534/http://www.cfl.ca/article/former-all-star-de-alex-hall-returns-to-riderville |archive-date=September 23, 2015 |access-date=August 24, 2017 |website=CFL.ca}}</ref>

'''Alexander Boone''' (born May 4, 1987) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Guard (gridiron football)|guard]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]]. He was signed by the [[San Francisco 49ers]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2009. He also played in the NFL with the [[Minnesota Vikings]], [[Arizona Cardinals]], and [[Seattle Seahawks]].

==Early life==
Boone played [[high school football]] at [[St. Edward High School (Lakewood, Ohio)|St. Edward High School]] in [[Lakewood, Ohio]], where he was a three-year starter and earned [[USA Today]] and [[Parade (magazine)|Parade]] All-American honors in his senior year. He was also a first-team All-Ohio selection in both his junior season in which St. Edward lost in the state championship game, and senior season. Following his high school career, Boone was invited to play in the [[U.S. Army All-American Bowl]] in December, and the following month he enrolled at Ohio State.

In addition to football, Boone also lettered in [[track & field]] for two years at St. Edward, throwing the [[shot put]] (personal-best of 56'1" or 14.05m) and the [[discus throw|discus]] and also played [[high school basketball|basketball]] for a year.

Boone committed to [[Ohio State University]] on January 8, 2003, during his junior year. Coming out of high school, Boone was considered one of the nation's top offensive line prospects and a Top-20 recruit by [[Rivals.com]]. Boone enrolled at Ohio State early (the start of Winter Quarter 2005) to get a head start.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://n.rivals.com/content/prospects/maple/21765 |title=Mitchell Crockum, 2010 Wide Receiver - Rivals.com |publisher=N.rivals.com |date=2010-02-08 |accessdate=2022-08-31}}</ref>

==College career==
A two-time All-Big Ten selection during his 4-year career at Ohio
State, Boone played [[college football]] at [[Ohio State University]], appearing in 46 games with 35 starts (22 of them at [[left tackle]]) for the Buckeyes. A four-year starter from 2005 to 2008, Boone was a two-time All-Big Ten selection (second-team in 2007 and first-team in 2008). In his four years with the Buckeyes, Ohio State compiled a 41–8 record and captured four [[Big Ten Conference]] titles and played in four BCS Bowl appearances.

===Freshman season (2005)===
{{see also|2005 Ohio State Buckeyes football team}}
As a freshman, Boone played in 11 of the Buckeyes' 12 games for a total of 126 minutes.

===Sophomore season (2006)===
{{see also|2006 Ohio State Buckeyes football team}}
In his second season, Boone started the first nine games at [[left tackle]], but missed the next two (Illinois in Week 10 and Northwestern in Week 11) before returning as a reserve against Michigan on November 18. He was back in the starting lineup in the national championship game. Boone was part of an offensive line that allowed just 12 sacks in the regular season and helped the Buckeyes average 229.7 yards passing per game and ran for 180.1 yards per game for an average of 409.8 total yards per game. He was named team's offensive lineman of the game against [[Penn State Nittany Lions football|Penn State]] in Week 4. The Buckeyes' offense racked up a season-high 540 yards against [[Indiana Hoosiers football|Indiana]] and 503 yards against [[Michigan Wolverines football|Michigan]] while also bettering 400 yards or more eight times.

===Junior season (2007)===
{{see also|2007 Ohio State Buckeyes football team}}
In his third-year as a starter at the left tackle position, Boone was named a second-team [[List of All-Big Ten Conference football teams|All-Big Ten]] by the media, coaches and Rivals. He was named offensive player of week following his performance in the game against [[Purdue Boilermakers football|Purdue]] in week 6. He was also named Jim Parker offensive lineman of the week for the Northwestern (week 4) and Penn State (week 9) games.

===Senior season (2008)===
{{see also|2008 Ohio State Buckeyes football team}}
As a senior in 2008, Boone was named first-team [[List of All-Big Ten Conference football teams|All-Big Ten]] and second-team [[Walter Camp Football Foundation]] All-America. In week 7, he suffered a stinger in the Purdue game. He was named Jim Parker offensive lineman of the week for the Youngstown State, Ohio, Wisconsin, Michigan State, Penn State and Illinois games. He was also recipient of the Jim Parker Award from Ohio State coaches. Following his senior season, Boone was invited to play in the [[East-West Shrine Game]].
